name: Merkin

lead: A merkin is a pubic wig, worn by women and men after shaving, for decorative or other purposes. It is a wig-like piece on a lace backing that gives the appearance of natural hair where the body has none.
Its best-known modern use is in film and television, where performers wear one to avoid full nudity while keeping a natural look. Some designers have also used the idea in fashion shows.

paras: It is attached to the skin with skin-safe adhesive such as spirit gum or wig tape applied to the lace backing, and is reusable and removable. Pieces are made in different colors to match the wearer or a character.
The main practical concern is skin reaction to adhesive. No clinical research exists on its use.

angle.text: It is a removable cosmetic covering that supplies the look of hair, matched in color to the wearer or character, without any change to the body.

lead: A merkin is a pubic wig. Wikipedia describes it as worn by women and men after shaving, for decorative or erotic purposes [1]. It attaches with skin-safe adhesive to a lace backing and can be removed and reused [1].

The Oxford Companion to the Body dates the pubic wig to the 1450s, though without a primary source, and links it to hygiene shaving against lice and to sex workers hiding signs of disease; the Oxford English Dictionary records the word from 1617 [1].
For looks, a merkin restores a natural pubic-hair appearance after shaving or for a costume, and in film it lets a performer appear natural while meeting nudity limits [1].
infobox: 1450s (Oxford Companion to the Body); word attested 1617

paras: A merkin is made on a lace base and applied with adhesive such as spirit gum or wig tape; it is reusable [1]. Grokipedia says historic examples used human, animal or goat hair and modern ones can be synthetic, though that source is AI-generated [2].

sections.h: Use in film, television and fashion
paras: Wikipedia lists performers who wore them, including Amy Landecker in A Serious Man (2009), where a 1967 setting made a clean-shaven look unlikely, and Rooney Mara in The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo (2011), whose piece was red to match the character [1]. Merkins also help productions avoid full-frontal nudity and so can aid a less restrictive rating [1].
In fashion, the design firm Neon used one on a nude model at São Paulo Fashion Week in 2010 to look more natural, per the designer [1].
